scope: Rank atoms and ions by size, ionisation energy, electron affinity and metallic character, and justify each ranking from nuclear charge and shielding.

formulas.n: S is shielding, dominated by core electrons. Across a period Z rises while S barely moves, so Z_eff rises and the atom contracts.

formulas.e: r \downarrow \mathrm{\ left\ to\ right}; \quad r \uparrow \mathrm{\ top\ to\ bottom}
formulas.n: Driven by Z_eff, not by electron count. A group going down adds a whole shell, so the increase always wins.
Same electron count only. O2- > F- > Ne > Na+ > Mg2+; comparing across different electron counts is meaningless.
Always gaseous and always endothermic. IE_2 > IE_1; only IE_1 follows the smooth periodic trend.
A jump after the 2nd electron means 2 valence electrons (group 2); after the 7th it means group 17.
Usually exothermic. EA(Cl) = -349 kJ/mol is MORE negative than EA(F) = -328 kJ/mol because F's compact 2p subshell repels the incoming electron.
Fluorine is the maximum. Values are dimensionless and relative, so only differences matter.
A rough cut: below about 0.4 largely covalent, above about 1.7 largely ionic. It is a continuum, not a boundary.
Caesium is the most metallic stable element; exam keys usually want Cs rather than the rarer, radioactive francium.
Similar charge-to-radius ratio gives similar chemistry (both Li and Mg form nitrides, both Be and Al are amphoteric).

traps: **Ranking ionisation energy by shell number alone.** Across period 3, $IE_1$ climbs from Na to Ar but dips at Al and at S: Al's third electron is removed from the higher-energy 3p, and S's from an already-paired 3p where repulsion assists removal. A clean left-to-right answer is wrong at exactly those two points.

**Ranking radius by electron count.** Cations are smaller and anions larger than their parent atom even though only the electron count changed; $\mathrm{Na^+}$ (10 e⁻) is smaller than $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ (18 e⁻) because $Z_{\mathrm{eff}}$ dominates. Any ranking built on 'more electrons means bigger' inverts.

**Assuming the top-right element has the largest electron affinity.** It does not: $EA(\mathrm{Cl}) = -349\ \mathrm{kJ/mol}$ beats $EA(\mathrm{F}) = -328\ \mathrm{kJ/mol}$ because fluorine's compact 2p subshell has strong inter-electron repulsion. Fluorine still wins on electronegativity, which is a different quantity.

**Treating shielding as a full electron count.** Only core electrons shield efficiently; same-shell electrons shield poorly. That is why $Z_{\mathrm{eff}}$ rises steeply across a period even though Z and the electron count each rise by one per element.
